content: 1. Identification of areas with a high risk of disease transmission is crucial for effective public health interventions. 2. Analyzing surveillance data based on the characteristics of affected individuals, such as age, sex, and religion, is essential. 3. Additional variables, including vaccination status, hospitalization history, and associated risk factors (e.g., recent travel, exposure in schools or workplaces), should also be considered to plan targeted interventions. 4. Data analysis can focus on confirmed cases (laboratory-confirmed and epidemiologically linked) or include all cases (laboratory-confirmed, epidemiologically linked, and possible cases). 5. When interpreting data, it is important to consider national or subnational vaccination coverage, vaccination schedules, and the types of pertussis-containing vaccines used. 6. Aggregated data should include the number of cases and incidence rates (if possible) by month, year, age group, and geographical area. Suggested age groupings may vary based on local priorities, such as <6 months, 6–11 months, 1–4 years, and ≥5 years. 7. The proportion of cases by the number of vaccine doses received, categorized by district and age group, should be analyzed. 8. The number of cases by pertussis immunization status (0, 1–2, 3+ doses) should also be included, if available. 9. Case-based data should include crude and age-specific case fatality ratios overall and by district. 10. Age-specific, sex-specific, and district-specific case numbers or incidence rates by month and year should be determined, provided population denominators are available. 11. The proportion of cases receiving antibiotics after diagnosis should be recorded. 12. The proportion of cases by final classification (laboratory-confirmed and epidemiologically linked) should be reported separately. 13. Regular monitoring of surveillance performance indicators can help identify areas of the surveillance and reporting system that require improvement. 14. If performance indicators are not being met, the reasons should be investigated and corrected. 15. During an outbreak, vaccination efforts should prioritize unvaccinated or under-immunized individuals. Routine immunization should also be strengthened in the outbreak area. 16. Vaccination campaigns are not typically part of the pertussis outbreak response. 17. In some countries, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) with macrolides is provided to asymptomatic household contacts or other close contacts of pertussis cases who are at the highest risk of developing clinical illness. 18. PEP may also be given to those at high risk of severe pertussis, such as infants, and to individuals who will have close contact with high-risk individuals. 19. Antibiotics may prevent pertussis disease if administered before symptom onset, but there is no evidence that widespread PEP use among contacts effectively controls or limits community-wide outbreaks. 20. PEP may be appropriate in limited, closed settings with a small number of identified cases and no ongoing community-wide outbreak. 21. Multiple rounds of antibiotics are not recommended in cases of continued pertussis transmission. 22. Active case search and contact tracing may not be the most effective use of limited public health resources during widespread community transmission of pertussis. 23. Active screening for symptomatic patients with suspected pertussis should be conducted during outbreaks in settings such as schools, daycare centers, and hospitals. 24. Active screening for suspected cases can reduce exposure to more individuals, particularly vulnerable infants. 25. The focus should be on the early treatment of infants under 6 months of age who show signs of respiratory illness. 26. All public and private health facilities in affected and surrounding areas must be notified and encouraged to maintain a high index of suspicion for pertussis cases. 27. Health promotion activities and the distribution of educational materials should provide basic information on pertussis and its prevention, particularly vaccination. 28. Pertussis, or whooping cough, is an acute bacterial disease of the respiratory tract caused by Bordetella pertussis. 29. The disease is common among children worldwide and is characterized by paroxysms of repeated violent coughing, often followed by a high-pitched inspiratory whoop. 30. Paroxysms may end with the expulsion of mucus, often followed by vomiting. Infants under 6 months may not exhibit typical paroxysms or the whoop. 31. Pertussis primarily affects infants and children but can also occur in teenagers and adults. 32. The disease spreads through direct contact with respiratory secretions, typically via large respiratory droplets generated by coughing or sneezing. 33. The incubation period is 9–10 days, with a range of 6–20 days. 34. Pertussis is not usually associated with fever and progresses through three stages: catarrhal, paroxysmal, and convalescent. 35. The catarrhal stage begins insidiously with an irritating cough that becomes paroxysmal over 1–2 weeks and lasts for 1–2 months or longer. 36. The paroxysmal stage involves repeated violent bursts of coughing, often within a single expiration, and may include cyanosis, vomiting, and the characteristic whoop. 37. The convalescent stage is marked by less frequent and less severe coughing. 38. Complications of pertussis include pneumonia (most common), seizures, encephalopathy (rare, usually in young infants), and death (most likely in unvaccinated infants). 39. Pertussis is highly contagious during the catarrhal stage, with a secondary attack rate of up to 90% among non-immune household contacts. 40. The case fatality ratio is highest in infants under 12 months, with an estimated average of 4%. 41. Two types of pertussis vaccines are available: whole-cell vaccines (wP) and acellular vaccines (aP). 42. Whole-cell vaccines are widely used in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) but have rare, significant side effects. 43. Acellular vaccines have fewer side effects and are effective, though less so than whole-cell vaccines. Many high-income countries (HICs) have replaced whole-cell vaccines with acellular formulations. 44. Despite high aP vaccine coverage, some HICs have experienced a resurgence of pertussis cases, linked to reduced vaccine efficacy and bacterial genetic evolution. 45. WHO recommends three doses of pertussis vaccine for all infants and one booster dose for children aged 1–6 years. 46. Surveillance for pertussis is suboptimal in many LMICs, leading to a lack of accurate epidemiological data. 47. Improved surveillance and data collection are needed to inform policy recommendations on booster doses and vaccination strategies. 48. Nasopharyngeal swabs (NPS) are the preferred specimen for pertussis diagnosis, and proper precautions should be taken during sample collection. 49. The procedure involves using a thin, flexible swab, measuring the appropriate insertion distance, and ensuring proper labeling and transport of the specimen.
